wstep: This card describes how to vine-dry beans grown for dry seeds (such as navy, kidney, lima), lentils and soybeans, finish drying them in a food dehydrator or oven and pasteurize them against insects.

akapity: Leave the pods on the vine until the beans rattle inside.
When the vines and pods are dry and shriveled, pick them and shell the beans.
Vine-dried beans need no pretreatment.
Moist beans must be dried further, or they will go mouldy.
Finish drying them in an oven or dehydrator.
In a dehydrator or oven, dry at 140 °F (60 °C).
Only use an oven if it can be set as low as 140 °F (60 °C); if it cannot go that low, the food cooks instead of drying.
Do not use trays or screens made of galvanized mesh; also avoid copper and aluminium mesh.
Pasteurize vine-dried beans against insects and their eggs: seal them in freezer bags and keep them in a freezer at 0 °F (-18 °C) or below for at least 48 hours.
Alternatively, spread them in a single layer in an oven preheated to 160 °F (about 71 °C) for 30 minutes.
Pack only completely cooled dried food: warm dried food sweats, and that moisture can be enough for mould to grow.
Dried food is susceptible to insects and moisture reabsorption, so once completely cool, pack it at once into clean, dry insect-proof containers, as tightly as possible without crushing.
Store dried food in clean, dry canning jars, plastic freezer containers with tight-fitting lids or plastic freezer bags.
Packaging must be food grade: do not use trash bags or plastic or fibreboard containers that previously held non-food items.
Pack amounts that can be used at one time: each opening exposes the dried food to air and moisture, which lowers quality and can lead to spoilage.
Vacuum packaging is not a preservation method by itself: removing oxygen increases the risk of botulism, and a product that needs refrigeration still needs it.
Store dried food in a cool, dry, dark place.
Check dried food often (glass shows condensation); if it has taken up moisture but is not spoiled, use it at once or dry it again and repack it.
Throw away mouldy dried food; also throw away any that smells off.

According to the FDA, raw or undercooked beans, particularly red kidney beans, can cause extreme nausea, severe vomiting and diarrhoea; proper cooking destroys the toxin, but slow cookers do not get hot enough to destroy it.

JarAtlas rule (cautious, after British studies cited by the FDA): before eating dried beans or soybeans from this card, soak them in water for at least 5 hours, pour the water away and boil them in fresh water for at least 30 minutes; do not cook them in a slow cooker.
